passage: As the daughter-in-law, I never told my husband Jagdish's parents that their unannounced visits drained me. I smiled, put the kettle on, and cancelled my plans, again and again. Each time the doorbell rang without a call, my jaw tightened. I told myself it was not worth a fuss. Then one Saturday his mother said, lightly, that the curtains looked dusty. I heard myself shouting that nobody in this house ever asked whether I wanted guests, and that I was tired of being on show. The room went silent. Jagdish stared at his plate. His mother left in tears before tea. The curtains were never the problem, and now everyone was hurt over words I had let pile up for a year. I wish I had spoken up on the first Sunday. - Kiran

Couples counsellor's note — Bidisha and Jeevan, first session, Kolkata.

They came in a week after what Jeevan called "the explosion".
For nearly a year, Jeevan's mother had dropped in without warning, sometimes three times a week, often at dinner time. Bidisha said nothing. She told me she didn't want to seem like the daughter-in-law who pushes family away. Instead she cleaned faster, cooked extra, and stayed quiet.
Last Sunday, her mother-in-law remarked that the curtains looked dusty. Bidisha shouted, cried, and said things about the whole year that she regretted immediately. Her mother-in-law left in tears. Jeevan's father has not phoned since.
"It wasn't about the curtains," Bidisha said here, very quietly. Jeevan looked stunned; he hadn't known she was unhappy at all.
What I did next: I asked each to write down, before next week, what they need from visits, so we can plan how to talk to his parents calmly.

qa.q: What did Bidisha's mother-in-law remark on last Sunday?
What did Bidisha mean by "It wasn't about the curtains"?
qa.a: She meant a year of silent resentment about the unannounced visits had built up, and the small comment simply set it off.

qa.q: What else could Bidisha have done early on, instead of saying nothing?
qa.a: She could have told Jeevan how the visits felt and agreed together on a kind way to ask his mother to call before coming.

qa.q: How is Jeevan affected by the outburst?
qa.a: Jeevan is stunned, since he had no idea Bidisha was unhappy, and now faces hurt on both sides of the family.

grounding: It shows a wife saying nothing about frequent unannounced visits until resentment builds and a minor comment triggers an outburst that hurts everyone.

passage:
Monday, 11 p.m.

I've ruined everything, and it started with a spoon.
Kashish, my sister-in-law, has been coming over with Maaji almost every evening since we moved in, without calling first. Every time, I smiled, put the kettle on, and said nothing. I thought keeping quiet was the respectful thing. Inside I was counting.
Tonight Maaji picked up the spoon I was stirring with and said, "Not like that." And I just... broke. I said they never give us any privacy. That I'm tired of pretending. That this doesn't feel like my home.
Maaji went pale. Kashish took her home without a word. My husband stood in the doorway looking at me like he didn't know me.
None of it was about a spoon. It was about a hundred evenings I never said anything.
I wish I'd said one small, kind thing in the first month.
— Kiran

qa.a: The spoon Kiran was stirring with.
Kiran feels ashamed and regretful, believing everything is ruined after months of quiet resentment burst out.

qa.q: What would you change first in Kiran's approach?
qa.a: In the first month, Kiran could have told the husband how the visits felt and agreed a kind request, such as calling before coming.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt taking Maaji home?
qa.a: Kashish was probably shocked and hurt, and protective of Maaji, not knowing how long the resentment had been building.

grounding: It shows a wife staying silent about frequent unannounced visits until resentment builds and a small comment causes an outburst that hurts everyone.
